svg.title: Microsoft Fabric Architecture Strategy — Operating Model to Migration Sequencing
svg.desc: An eight-node architecture diagram. A tenant-domain-workspace containment hierarchy feeds role-oriented workloads such as Data Factory, Data Warehouse, and Power BI, which all persist to the shared OneLake platform layer. From OneLake, two governance and compute boundaries branch off: a three-tier governance hierarchy backed by Purview, and capacity isolation split by environment stage. The tenant hierarchy also feeds governance and capacity directly. Capacity feeds Deployment Pipelines, which promote items Dev to Test to Production. Governance feeds a network-isolation decision comparing tenant-wide and workspace-level private links. Both deployment pipelines and the network-isolation decision converge on a closing SaaS framing node stating there is no separate infrastructure layer underneath any of these decisions.
svg.text: Fabric Architecture Strategy — operating model to migration sequencing
Tenant/domain/workspace hierarchy · shared OneLake · governance & capacity boundaries · deployment pipelines · network isolation

g.title: Tenant → domain → workspace hierarchy — One Fabric tenant maps 1:1 to one Microsoft Entra tenant; domains group workspaces for delegated governance; workspaces hold items and draw compute from a capacity.

Role-oriented workloads over one OneLake — Data Factory, Data Warehouse, Power BI, and other role-oriented workloads create items inside a workspace; every workload persists its data to the same tenant-wide OneLake.
g.text: each creates its own item types inside the workspace
…and more — each workload is an execution engine, not a separate storage silo

g.title: OneLake: the shared storage layer — OneLake is the tenant-wide logical data lake every workload writes to and reads from; the shared platform layer the whole hierarchy above is built to feed.
g.text: Tenant-wide logical data lake · open Delta Parquet
Every workload's items land here, addressable
by every compute engine — no per-workload copy

svg.text: governance attaches at the platform boundary
02 · GOVERNANCE & CAPACITY BOUNDARIES ATTACHED TO ONELAKE

g.aria-label: Governance: tenant, domain, workspace policy via Purview
g.title: Governance: tenant → domain → workspace policy — Purview-backed governance operates as a three-tier hierarchy: tenant-wide defaults, domain-level overrides, and workspace-level controls covering data-estate management, protection, discovery, and monitoring.
g.text: Three-tier policy hierarchy resolves per item:

g.title: Capacity: environment & workload isolation — Capacities are the compute isolation and chargeback boundary; the documented pattern splits capacities by environment stage and reserves separate capacity for contention-sensitive workloads.
g.text: Split by environment stage · chargeback boundary

svg.text: network isolation is a governance/security decision
03 · RELEASE PATH & A REAL ARCHITECTURE FORK

g.aria-label: Deployment Pipelines: Dev to Test to Production
g.title: Deployment Pipelines: Dev → Test → Production — Items are promoted across Dev, Test, and Production workspaces through Deployment Pipelines, with Variable Libraries injecting per-environment connection strings and pull-request gates before production promotion.
g.text: Variable Libraries swap per-environment connection strings at each promotion step
Approved pull request required before Test → Production promotion executes

g.aria-label: Network isolation decision: tenant-wide vs workspace-level private link
g.title: Network isolation: tenant-wide vs workspace-level private link — Tenant-wide private links are all-or-nothing and break on-premises gateways; workspace-level private links (F-SKU only) allow a mixed public/private deployment instead.
g.text: need it, keep the rest public
IP firewall absent a regulatory mandate

svg.text: promotion needs no infrastructure provisioning step

g.aria-label: SaaS: no separate infrastructure layer to provision
g.title: SaaS: no separate infrastructure layer — Because Fabric is a single SaaS control plane, none of the decisions above involve provisioning Azure resource groups, ARM templates, or redundancy settings underneath.
g.text: Fabric is SaaS — no separate infrastructure layer underneath
Every decision above (tenant/domain/workspace, governance, capacity, pipelines, network isolation)
is configuration and policy, not Azure resource-group, ARM template, or VNet provisioning
